title: Sequential Recommendation & Slate Diversification
text:
A Practice-Oriented AI project investigating sequential recommendation and slate diversification using the MovieLens dataset.
The work compared modern recommendation approaches and investigated Maximum Marginal Relevance (MMR) for controlling the trade-off between recommendation relevance and diversity, both within individual recommendation slates and across successive sessions.
The project explored matrix-factorisation and sequential recommendation approaches alongside Transformer-based and generative recommendation models, with evaluation focused on ranking quality and diversification.

title: Research
text:
My research lies at the intersection of multimodal artificial intelligence, computer vision, robotics, and autonomous systems. I am interested in developing intelligent systems that can integrate complementary sources of information, reason across space and time, and understand their interactions with complex real-world environments.
My work broadly spans three connected themes:

title: Research
text:
Current Research

Multimodal Spatiotemporal Learning of UAV–Environment Interactions
My current research investigates how autonomous aerial systems can perceive and understand their interactions with complex atmospheric environments. Using operational fixed-wing UAV flights through volcanic plumes, I combine onboard video and aircraft telemetry to model the evolving relationship between the aircraft and its environment.
The problem is currently formulated around four temporally structured interaction states:
Approaching → Entering → Inside → Exiting
Rather than treating individual observations independently, the work investigates how visual appearance, temporal context, and changes in aircraft state can jointly characterise these interactions.
Current approaches include vision transformers, video-native spatiotemporal models, telemetry transformers, cross-attention, and residual-gated multimodal fusion. A central question is how complementary aircraft-state information can improve perception while preserving strong representations learned from vision.
This research provides a real-world setting for investigating broader questions in multimodal learning, temporal perception, sensor fusion, and autonomous-system interaction understanding.

title: Research
text:
Emerging Research Direction

From Interaction Recognition to Dynamic 3D/4D Environment Understanding
An emerging direction of my research is moving beyond the classification of discrete interaction states towards explicit spatial and temporal modelling of autonomous systems and the dynamic environments through which they move.
I am interested in representations that can capture not only what an autonomous platform observes, but also where structures exist in 3D space, how they evolve over time, and how the platform’s own motion relates to those changes.
This motivates exploring modern approaches to 3D and 4D scene representation and reconstruction, including 3D Gaussian Splatting and dynamic/4D Gaussian representations, alongside neural and geometry-aware methods for dynamic scene reconstruction, novel-view synthesis, and spatiotemporal representation learning.
For UAV–environment interactions, such representations could potentially move the problem from:
“What interaction state is the UAV currently in?”
towards richer questions such as:
“What is the evolving 3D structure of the environment, how is the UAV moving relative to it, and how is that interaction changing through time?”
The longer-term goal is to investigate whether these richer world representations can support environment understanding, interaction modelling, prediction, and ultimately more informed autonomous decision-making in complex dynamic environments.

title: Research
text:
Previous Research
My previous research spans several areas that provide the foundation for my current work.

Robotic Perception
Research on multisensor perception for autonomous ground robots, including camera and LiDAR-based environmental perception, sensor alignment, semantic understanding, and autonomous navigation.


Computer Vision & AI
Research in computer vision and machine learning, including spatiotemporal visual learning, human activity understanding, and intelligent perception from visual and depth-sensing data.


UAV Systems
Practical work involving UAV development, autopilot systems, system integration, and flight testing, providing experience with the physical platforms and sensing systems underlying autonomous aerial operations.


Spacecraft Guidance & Control
Research in spacecraft attitude determination and control, including fault-tolerant and adaptive control approaches, attitude-control modes, and control of small spacecraft systems.

My research increasingly brings these areas together around a central question:
“How can intelligent autonomous systems build useful representations of complex environments and understand their own interactions with them?”

title: Multimodal Spatiotemporal Learning of UAV–Environment Interactions
text:
Dataset
The work uses data collected during fixed-wing UAV flights at Volcán de Fuego, Guatemala. The dataset contains multiple independent encounters with volcanic plumes, with video and aircraft telemetry recorded during flight.
Interaction periods were temporally annotated and partitioned by flight before observation windows were generated, reducing the risk of information leakage between training, validation, and test data.

title: Multimodal Spatiotemporal Learning of UAV–Environment Interactions
text:
Approach
The project develops a multimodal framework for learning UAV–environment interactions from complementary visual and aircraft-state information.

Spatiotemporal visual perception
Onboard video is used to learn representations of the evolving visual interaction between the UAV and its environment. Rather than relying only on individual frames, the approach incorporates temporal context to capture changes in appearance and interaction dynamics over an observation period.


Aircraft-state representation
Synchronised aircraft telemetry provides a complementary view of the interaction through the physical state and response of the UAV. Temporal representations are learned from selected flight signals, enabling changes in aircraft behaviour to be considered alongside the visual observations.


Multimodal representation and fusion
The visual and aircraft-state representations are integrated through cross-modal learning, allowing information from one modality to contextualise and complement the other. The current approach explores attention-based fusion with a residual-gated pathway designed to incorporate useful telemetry information while preserving strong visual representations.
Together, these components investigate whether the interaction between an autonomous platform and its environment can be better understood by jointly modelling what the platform sees and how it responds over time.

title: Multimodal Spatiotemporal Learning of UAV–Environment Interactions
text:
Research Questions
The project explores broader questions including:

How much information about an environmental interaction can be inferred from vision alone?
What complementary information is contained in aircraft telemetry?
When does multimodal fusion improve perception over a strong visual model?
How should heterogeneous modalities with different temporal characteristics be aligned and fused?
How can temporal structure and physically plausible state transitions contribute to interaction understanding?

title: Multimodal Spatiotemporal Learning of UAV–Environment Interactions
text:
Towards Dynamic Environment Modelling
The longer-term direction extends beyond discrete interaction-state recognition towards richer spatial and temporal representations of UAV–environment interactions.
This motivates investigation of modern 3D and 4D scene-representation approaches, including Gaussian Splatting and dynamic scene reconstruction, to represent the evolving geometry and appearance of complex environments together with the motion of the observing platform.

title: GeoAI for Geospatial Change Detection
text:
A collaborative research project with Ordnance Survey exploring the use of artificial intelligence and computer vision for geospatial change detection and map-update workflows.
The project investigated learning from geospatial imagery and mapping information in real-world settings, with particular interest in reliable change identification and the challenges introduced by imperfect, heterogeneous, and temporally varying data.

title: Spacecraft Attitude Control & Autonomous Space Systems
text:
Research spanning spacecraft attitude determination and control, fault-tolerant control, and autonomous small-spacecraft systems.
The work includes the development and investigation of fault-tolerant and adaptive attitude-control approaches, anti-windup control, and attitude-control modes for small spacecraft.
Related research has included work on the ESTCube-2 attitude determination and control system and ESTCube-LuNa, including control and mission considerations associated with small-spacecraft and Electric Solar Wind Sail technologies.

title: Ikechukwu Ofodile
text:
Ike is a PhD student in the UKRI AI Centre for Doctoral Training in Practice-Oriented Artificial Intelligence at the University of Bristol. His research focuses on multimodal perception, computer vision, and spatiotemporal learning for autonomous systems. He is particularly interested in developing AI systems that combine visual and onboard sensor information to understand complex and dynamic environments.
His current research explores UAV–environment interaction, using video and aircraft telemetry to understand and model how unmanned aerial vehicles interact with challenging atmospheric environments. His recent work investigates UAV–volcanic plume interactions, including multimodal learning of the different stages of interaction and, more broadly, how these interactions can be represented and modelled for autonomous perception.
Before joining the University of Bristol, Ike conducted research at the University of Tartu spanning autonomous systems, artificial intelligence, computer vision, and spacecraft control. Working with Prof. Andris Slavinskis and Prof. Gholamreza Anbarjafari (Shahab), his research included fault-tolerant spacecraft attitude control, robotic perception, and computer vision. His broader work in autonomous systems has also included UAV development, autopilot systems, and flight testing. He also completed an MSc in Robotics and Computer Engineering at the University of Tartu, graduating cum laude (with distinction).
